# Train Your AI Agent with SkillOpt: A Step‑by‑Step Guide

**Hook:** By the end of this guide you’ll have added a brand‑new “skill” to your SkillOpt AI agent, so it can perform a task you choose – for example summarising a handful of emails or drafting a short social‑media post. This is written for anyone who’s new to AI agents and wants a practical, hands‑on result.

## Before you start
- A **SkillOpt account** (sign‑up is free; you’ll need an email and a password).  
- Access to the **SkillOpt website** on a computer or tablet with a modern web browser.  
- An **existing AI agent** already created in SkillOpt – you can use the default “Assistant” that comes with a new account.  
- A **clear, single task** you want the agent to learn (e.g., “turn a product review into a one‑sentence summary”).  
- About **30 minutes** of uninterrupted time to follow the steps, add a few training examples, and test the new skill.  

*Note:* SkillOpt can generate text for you, but it cannot automatically send emails, post to social media, or interact with external apps unless you add extra integrations later.

## Step 1 — Open the SkillOpt dashboard and pick your agent
**Action:** Log into the SkillOpt website (https://app.skillopt.com) and click the tile that shows the name of the AI agent you want to train.  
**What you see:** After signing in, a main dashboard appears with a horizontal row of tiles labelled with your agents’ names; each tile displays a small avatar and a brief description.  
**What happens next:** Clicking the tile opens a dedicated control panel for that agent, showing tabs such as “Overview”, “Skills”, and “Settings”.  
**If it looks different:** If you don’t see tiles, look for a menu labelled “My Agents”, “Agent Hub”, or a sidebar icon shaped like a person; clicking that should list all your agents.  
💬 Example: *No typing is required in this step; just use your mouse or touchpad to click the agent named “Assistant”.*  
**Success check:** You’ll know it worked when the screen displays the chosen agent’s name at the top and a list of its current skills underneath.

## Step 2 — Clarify the new skill’s input and output
**Action:** Write down, in a simple notebook or a digital note, what information you will give the agent (the **input**) and what you expect it to return (the **output**).  
**What you see:** Your note will have two short sentences, for example: “Input: a product review paragraph. Output: a one‑sentence summary that captures the overall rating.”  
**What happens next:** This written definition guides every later step, keeping the skill focused and easy for the AI to learn.  
**If it looks different:** If you prefer typing, open a blank document in any editor; the important part is that you have a concrete pair of sentences you can copy later.  
💬 Example: *Input – “Customer feedback: the product is fast but the battery dies quickly.” Output – “The product is speedy, but its battery life is short.”*  
**Success check:** You’ll know it worked when you can point to a clear input‑output pair that describes exactly one task you want the agent to perform.

## Step 3 — Add a new skill entry in SkillOpt
**Action:** In the agent’s control panel, locate and click the button that says **“Add New Skill”** (or a similar plus‑icon).  
**What you see:** A modal window or new page appears with fields labelled “Skill Name” and “Skill Description”.  
**What happens next:** After you fill the fields and confirm, SkillOpt creates a blank skill ready for training data.  
**If it looks different:** If you don’t see “Add New Skill”, look for a tab called “Skills” and then a plus‑sign or a link that says “Create Skill”. Some layouts use a gear‑icon next to the skill list.  
💬 Example: *Skill Name – “Review Summariser”. Skill Description – “Takes a short product review as input and returns a one‑sentence summary that reflects the overall sentiment.”*  
**Success check:** You’ll know it worked when the new skill appears in the list, usually with the name you entered and a status like “No training data yet”.

## Step 4 — Upload an input example for the skill
**Action:** Click the “Add Input Example” button inside the newly created skill’s page and paste a real example of the text you will give the agent.  
**What you see:** An empty text box appears, often titled “Input Example” or “Sample Input”.  
**What happens next:** After you paste the example and press “Save” or “Add”, the system stores this snippet as part of the skill’s training set.  
**If it looks different:** If the button is labelled “New Input” or the box is under a heading called “Training Data”, use that instead – the aim is to get a text field where you can type or paste.  
💬 Example: *Input Example – “I love the camera quality, but the phone overheats after a few minutes of video playback.”*  
**Success check:** You’ll know it worked when the input you entered shows up in a list of examples, usually with a short preview of the first few words.

## Step 5 — Provide the matching expected output
**Action:** While still viewing the same example, locate the adjacent “Expected Output” field and type the exact response you want the agent to produce for that input.  
**What you see:** A second text box, often directly below the input box, labelled “Output Example”, “Desired Result”, or “Correct Response”.  
**What happens next:** Saving this pair tells SkillOpt what the ideal answer looks like; the platform will use it to fine‑tune the underlying model.  
**If it looks different:** Some interfaces use a “+” icon to attach an output to an input, or a dropdown to select “Add Output”. Choose whichever option lets you type a response that pairs with the earlier input.  
💬 Example: *Expected Output – “The camera is excellent, but the device runs hot during video playback.”*  
**Success check:** You’ll know it worked when the input and output appear side‑by‑side in the training list, typically displayed as “Input → Output”.

## Step 6 — Test the skill and activate it
**Action:** Press the “Test Skill” or “Run Test” button (often at the top or bottom of the skill page) and paste a fresh piece of text that follows the same pattern as your training input.  
**What you see:** A blank testing field appears, prompting you to enter new input; after you click “Generate” you’ll see a response appear in an output pane.  
**What happens next:** SkillOpt runs the trained model on your new input; the generated text should mirror the style and structure of your expected outputs.  
**If it looks different:** If the button reads “Preview”, “Run”, or is represented by a play‑icon (►), click that instead – the goal is to trigger a one‑off generation.  
💬 Example: *Test Input – “The laptop is lightweight, but the battery drains quickly when I run Photoshop.”*  
**Success check:** You’ll know it worked when the output reads something like “The laptop is portable, yet its battery life drops fast during heavy Photoshop use,” matching the format you defined. If the result looks off, repeat Steps 4 and 5 with additional examples until the test output feels reliable, then click the final “Activate” or “Publish” button to make the skill available to your agent.

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake:** *Writing a vague description such as “summarise text”.*  
  **Fix:** Include specific instructions (“summarise into one sentence and add a sentiment tag”). The clearer the description, the better the AI learns.  
- **Mistake:** *Providing only one or two input‑output pairs.*  
  **Fix:** Add at least three varied examples covering different wording styles; this helps the model generalise to new inputs.  
- **Mistake:** *Inconsistent formatting between outputs (sometimes bullets, sometimes paragraphs).*  
  **Fix:** Pick one format (e.g., a single sentence) and use it for every example; consistency prevents the AI from mixing styles.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** You can give your SkillOpt assistant the ability to turn long product reviews, news snippets, or chat messages into tidy one‑line summaries, saving you time when you skim information.  
- **For your business or work:** A customised skill can automate routine reporting – for instance, summarising daily sales notes into a quick executive brief, freeing up staff for higher‑value work.  
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with a very simple skill like “turn a single paragraph into a headline”; once you’re comfortable, expand to multi‑step abilities such as “extract key dates and format them as a calendar list”.

## Try it now
Pick a short piece of text you frequently read (a recent email, a product review, or a news headline). Follow Steps 1‑6 to create a skill called “Quick Summary” and test it with that text – you’ll see the new ability in action within two minutes.
